rows.source: HSE scaffolding safety guidance
rows.verified: Scaffolds should be designed, erected, altered and dismantled only by competent people under a competent supervisor.

rows.source: HSE scaffolding safety guidance
rows.verified: Scaffolding from which a person might fall 2 metres or more must be inspected on completion and at least weekly thereafter.

rows.source: HSE scaffolding safety guidance
rows.verified: Further scaffold inspection may be required after bad weather and must be carried out after modification.

rows.source: HSE scaffolding safety guidance
rows.verified: A visible tag system can supplement inspection records but is not itself a legal substitute for inspection and reporting.

rows.source: HSE scaffolding safety guidance
rows.verified: Scaffold erection and alteration should prioritise collective fall protection and minimise reliance on personal fall-arrest equipment.

rows.source: HSE scaffolding safety guidance
rows.verified: People erecting tower scaffolds should be competent and trained under an appropriate recognised industry or manufacturer scheme.

rows.source: HSE scaffolding safety guidance
rows.verified: The permitted height and configuration of a tower scaffold must follow the manufacturer’s instructions.

rows.source: HSE scaffolding safety guidance
rows.verified: Construction sites must prevent unauthorised access to scaffolds and access ladders, including through fencing, ladder removal or suitable locked guards.

rows.source: HSE scaffolding safety guidance
rows.verified: Scaffold safety depends on design, foundations, ties, loading, erection sequence, inspection history, weather, modification, access control and user behaviour.

rows.source: HSE scaffolding safety guidance
rows.verified: General competent design, erection, inspection, fall protection and access security for scaffolds guidance does not prove current conditions or control performance at an individual parcel and does not establish an exact incident, exposure or illness probability.

rows.source: HSE ladder and stepladder safety guidance
rows.verified: Ladders are not banned, but should be used only where a risk assessment shows they are suitable for the task.

rows.source: HSE ladder and stepladder safety guidance
rows.verified: A ladder can be appropriate for low-risk, short-duration work or where existing workplace features prevent use of higher-protection equipment.

rows.source: HSE ladder and stepladder safety guidance
rows.verified: Short duration alone does not justify ladder use; as a guide, work lasting more than 30 minutes on a ladder should prompt consideration of alternative equipment.

rows.source: HSE ladder and stepladder safety guidance
rows.verified: Ladders should be used only where they can be level, stable and secured so far as reasonably practicable.

rows.source: HSE ladder and stepladder safety guidance
rows.verified: Users must be competent or work under the supervision of a competent person while being trained.

rows.source: HSE ladder and stepladder safety guidance
rows.verified: Ladders should receive a pre-use check each working day and regular detailed visual inspections by a competent person.

rows.source: HSE ladder and stepladder safety guidance
rows.verified: Leaning ladders should be tied at both stiles, secured with a stability device or wedged; footing is a last resort.

rows.source: HSE ladder and stepladder safety guidance
rows.verified: Access ladders should normally extend at least one metre above the landing, and leaning ladders should be positioned near the 1-in-4 angle without overreaching or working from the top three rungs.

rows.source: HSE ladder and stepladder safety guidance
rows.verified: Ladder risk depends on task duration and force, ladder type and condition, ground, angle, securing, access height, weather, carried loads and user competence.

rows.source: HSE ladder and stepladder safety guidance
rows.verified: General selection, competence, pre-use checks, securing, positioning and inspection of ladders guidance does not prove current conditions or control performance at an individual parcel and does not establish an exact incident, exposure or illness probability.
